strengths: Introduces a genuinely more general formulation than prior work: a latent-conditioned deformation field that can model an arbitrary number of interaction states and an arbitrary number of movable parts without requiring the part count to be specified in advance, unlike PARIS/ArticulatedGS (single joint, two states) and DTArt/ArtGS (fixed part count, two states).

The trajectory-based coarse clustering combined with visibility-aware SAM prompting and boundary-aware Gaussian splitting is a sensible and technically detailed pipeline for turning noisy motion cues into clean part boundaries; the refinement ablation (Table 5, Fig. 5) convincingly shows its benefit.

Extensive experiments: an enlarged PartNet-Mobility split (more instances per category, 2- and 3-part objects), a new real-to-sim dataset (RS-Art) with reverse-engineered URDF/USD assets, and multiple ablations (refinement stage, number of interaction states K) that are individually informative.

Demonstrates useful downstream capabilities beyond reconstruction, including joint-type classification, joint parameter estimation, and interpolation to unseen articulation states, which is not shown by most competing baselines.
The RS-Art dataset, if released, could be a valuable community resource given the scarcity of real-world articulated object benchmarks with precise ground-truth kinematics.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol in Table 1 reports only the 'first run' of baselines due to observed run-to-run variance, rather than mean ± std over multiple runs; this is a non-standard and somewhat questionable choice that could bias comparisons even if not intentionally cherry-picked, and undermines confidence in the reported margins.

The claim of being 'fully self-supervised' / requiring 'no human annotation' is in tension with the reliance on an external VLM for estimating the number of parts and SAM for mask refinement — both are pretrained models with their own biases/failure modes, and the paper provides no sensitivity analysis of how VLM miscounts affect final performance beyond a majority-vote heuristic.

RS-Art is fairly small in scale (18 objects across 6 categories, 3 instances each), which limits statistical power and diversity for the very real-to-sim generalization claim the dataset is meant to support.
No analysis of computational cost/runtime/training time relative to baselines, which matters given the added complexity of the deformation network, clustering, VLM/SAM calls, and recursive splitting.

Recent related 3DGS-based articulation methods mentioned in the related work (e.g., ReArtGS) are not included as quantitative baselines, leaving open how DeGSS compares to the most recent competitive work.

The method still assumes accurate known camera poses and cannot handle fully occluded regions, as acknowledged, and there is no experiment testing robustness to pose noise despite this being flagged as a limitation.

Several technical choices (motion threshold τ_mot, visibility margin τ_vis=1.2, 2% noise-cluster merging threshold) appear to be manually tuned hyperparameters without ablation or justification of sensitivity, which raises reproducibility/robustness concerns across diverse object categories.

strengths: The core idea of representing all interaction states as deformations of a single canonical 3D Gaussian field, indexed by a latent code, is a reasonable generalization beyond the restrictive 'two-state, one-part' assumption of prior PARIS/ArticulatedGS/DTArt/ArtGS pipelines, and in principle removes the need to pre-specify the number of parts.

The coarse-to-fine segmentation pipeline (motion-based clustering followed by visibility-aware SAM prompting and boundary-aware Gaussian splitting) is a sensible way to combine motion cues with appearance-based segmentation priors.

The proposed RS-Art dataset, with paired real RGB-D captures and reverse-engineered URDF/USD digital twins across six categories, addresses a genuine gap in evaluating real-to-sim transfer for articulated object reconstruction, which prior work largely ignored.

The experimental section includes a reasonably broad battery of metrics (axis angle/position, part motion error, several Chamfer distance variants) and several ablations (refinement stage, number of interaction states K), as well as qualitative visualizations of latent-code interpolation to unseen states.
The paper is upfront about limitations (occlusion, lack of physical properties, difficulty with screw joints), which is appreciated.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocol fairness is questionable: the authors explicitly report only the 'first run' of baselines to 'reveal variance,' rather than averaging over multiple runs or reporting standard deviations, which is non-standard practice and risks biasing comparisons against baselines while the paper simultaneously claims superior 'stability' for its own method without analogous multi-run statistics for DeGSS itself.

The comparison protocol differs substantially across methods (single-joint baselines run once per joint with 200 images per part, i.e., 200×n_parts total images, while DTArt/ArtGS get 200 images total and DeGSS also gets 200 images spread over 4 states); although the paper claims this equalizes the 'per-run' budget, the total information available to different methods is not actually matched, which confounds the comparison.

A directly relevant and recent 3DGS-based baseline mentioned in related work, ReArtGS, is omitted from all quantitative comparisons without justification, weakening the claim of comprehensive SOTA comparison.

The pipeline depends on several hand-tuned thresholds (τ_mot for motion/static separation, τ_vis=1.2 for visibility dominance, 2% noise-cluster merging threshold, rank-ratio 0.05 for revolute/prismatic classification) with no sensitivity analysis or justification of these specific values, raising concerns about robustness and generalizability to new object classes.

The number-of-parts estimation relies on querying a VLM with a fixed prompt and taking the mode over sampled image pairs; no quantitative evaluation of VLM accuracy/failure modes is provided, and this component is a potential silent failure point for the 'fully self-supervised' claim.

The RS-Art benchmark, while a nice contribution, is small (18 objects, 3 per category across 6 categories), which limits its statistical power and its value as a rigorous large-scale benchmark, somewhat undercutting the paper's own critique of prior PartNet-Mobility evaluations as being too limited.
The K-states ablation (Table 6) is conducted on a single object (Door 9168), which is insufficient to support general claims about how performance scales with the number of interaction states.

Mesh extraction quality (TSDF fusion + marching cubes) is not separately validated against ground-truth meshes beyond the aggregate Chamfer metrics already reported, and no runtime/computational cost comparisons are given despite the added complexity of VLM queries, SAM prompting, and recursive Gaussian splitting relative to baselines.

The manuscript contains multiple writing/typesetting issues (e.g., unclear equation around Eq. 7 'minimizing the results', inconsistent notation such as α used both for opacity and latent code, 'inteactive state' typo) that reduce clarity and suggest the paper would benefit from a more careful revision pass.
The method assumes accurate known camera poses and offers no empirical test of robustness to pose noise, which is a common real-world scenario explicitly acknowledged as unaddressed.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated limitation of prior work: existing NeRF/3DGS articulated-object methods assume either a single joint observed in exactly two states (PARIS, ArticulatedGS) or a known part count with two closely-aligned states (DTArt, ArtGS). DeGSS removes both restrictions via a latent-conditioned deformation field that can ingest an arbitrary number of interaction states and automatically infer the number of parts.

Technically coherent multi-stage pipeline: deformable Gaussian field for joint geometry/appearance/kinematics modeling, motion-driven coarse clustering via trajectory descriptors, VLM-based automatic part-count estimation, and SAM-guided boundary-aware Gaussian splitting for refined part boundaries — each stage is clearly motivated and ablated.

Introduces RS-Art, a new real-to-sim dataset pairing real RGB-D captures with accurately reverse-engineered, physically grounded digital twins (URDF/USD) across six object categories, which is a valuable and reusable community resource that helps bridge the sim-to-real gap in this subfield.

Extends PartNet-Mobility evaluation beyond the previously common single-object-per-category protocol, improving statistical robustness of comparisons, and additionally reports results on objects with three movable parts to test scalability.

Extensive and mostly convincing experiments: comparisons against four recent SOTA baselines across many joint/geometry metrics, ablations on the refinement stage (quantitative and qualitative), ablation on number of interaction states K, real-world validation, and demonstration of generalization to unseen interaction states via latent interpolation — a capability none of the baselines exhibit.

Results show consistent, often large, improvements over baselines in most metrics on both synthetic and real data, and the method appears markedly more stable (baselines show high run-to-run variance and frequent failures, denoted by asterisks in Table 1).
weaknesses: The fairness of the baseline comparison protocol is debatable: single-joint and two-state baselines are restricted by design to fewer interaction states while DeGSS is given four states; although image budgets are equalized, DeGSS's core innovation (leveraging many states for trajectory disambiguation, as shown in the K-ablation in the appendix) is inherently advantaged by this setup, making the comparison somewhat asymmetric in favor of the proposed method.

The VLM-based part-count estimation (nparts) and motion/visibility thresholds (τmot, τvis) are important but under-analyzed hyperparameters/design choices; there is no reported accuracy or failure analysis of the VLM step, nor sensitivity analysis of the thresholds, despite these being critical for correct downstream clustering and segmentation.

RS-Art is relatively small (18 objects, 3 per category across 6 categories), and in the real-data evaluation only ArtGS could be run reliably as a baseline, limiting the strength of real-world comparative claims; other baselines' failures on real data are not analyzed in detail.

Performance is not uniformly best across all metrics (e.g., CD-w in several PartNet-Mobility categories and some RS-Art categories favor DTArt or ArtGS), and the paper does not discuss why these specific metrics/objects are harder for DeGSS.

No runtime, memory, or computational cost comparison is provided, despite the added complexity of the deformation network, VLM querying, SAM prompting, and recursive Gaussian splitting relative to simpler baselines.

The method still assumes accurate calibrated camera poses per state and explicit multi-view multi-state captures, which is acknowledged as a limitation but somewhat tempers the 'fully self-supervised' framing given the reliance on external SfM/VLM/SAM modules as non-differentiable, off-the-shelf components.

Minor clarity issues: some equation/notation inconsistencies (e.g., Eq. 7 labeled 'results' rather than 'loss', inconsistent latent symbol usage α vs z), and some qualitative figures/discussion could benefit from more quantitative failure-case analysis of the VLM part-counting and clustering steps.

strengths: Novel formulation that models articulated object interaction states as continuous deformations of a shared canonical Gaussian field, rather than relying on pairwise/discrete state matching, which is a meaningful departure from prior PARIS/DTArt/ArtGS-style approaches and naturally supports an arbitrary number of interaction states and parts without requiring the part count to be known a priori.

The coarse-to-fine part segmentation (motion-trajectory clustering + VLM-based part count estimation + visibility-aware SAM prompting + boundary-aware Gaussian splitting) is a reasonable and largely self-supervised pipeline for turning motion cues into clean part boundaries, and ablations (Tab. 11, 13, 14, 15) support the contribution of each stage.

Release of RS-Art, a real-to-sim RGB-D dataset with reverse-engineered, part-annotated 3D models in URDF format, addresses a genuine gap (most prior work evaluates only 1 instance/category on synthetic PartNet-Mobility) and could be a useful community resource.

Extensive experimentation: comparisons against single-joint (PARIS, ArticulatedGS), multi-joint (DTArt, ArtGS), dynamic-scene (D-NeRF, D2NeRF, Dynamic3DGS, 4D-GS), and generative (NAP, SINGAPO) baselines; ablations on number of interaction states, refinement stage, camera pose noise robustness, and per-module quantitative analysis in the appendix.

Demonstrated qualitative and quantitative ability to interpolate/generalize to unseen interaction states while keeping multiple parts independently controllable, which is a practically useful property for digital-twin and continuous-control applications that most baselines (e.g., PARIS) fail to achieve cleanly.
weaknesses: The pipeline contains numerous hand-tuned thresholds and heuristics (τmot for motion detection, τvis for visibility-based SAM prompting, 2% noise-cluster merging, fixed numbers of FPS positive/negative prompts, VLM prompt wording, rank-based joint-type threshold r<0.05), several of which are described as "tuned on one or two representative instances" — this raises concerns about generalizability and reproducibility across novel object categories not seen during tuning.

The main quantitative comparison (Tab. 1) reports only the "first run" of baselines due to high run-to-run variance, which, while transparently disclosed, makes it harder to assess whether the reported gains are robust versus favorable seeding; averaging over multiple seeds with variance bars would be more convincing.

The overall system is a complex multi-stage pipeline with non-differentiable post-processing (clustering, VLM querying, SAM prompting, recursive Gaussian splitting) sitting between differentiable modules; error propagation/failure analysis across these stages (beyond the single refinement ablation) is limited, and the interaction between coarse segmentation accuracy and final geometry/kinematic accuracy is not deeply analyzed.

RS-Art, while valuable, is still fairly small in scale (18 objects, 6 categories, 3 instances/category), which limits its capacity to serve as a comprehensive real-world benchmark and leaves open questions about generalization to more diverse geometries, materials, and articulation types (e.g., screw joints, which the paper explicitly acknowledges as unhandled).

Reliance on a VLM for estimating the number of moving parts introduces an external, potentially brittle dependency; although ablations (Tab. 13) show near-perfect accuracy on the tested categories, this may not hold for more cluttered or ambiguous real-world scenes, and the method's overall part-decoupling quality is contingent on this initial estimate being correct.

The paper does not model physical properties (mass, friction, joint limits robustness) and has limited ability to reason about joint types/limits from sparse states, restricting its direct applicability to physics-based simulation despite motivating digital-twin use cases; these are acknowledged but not addressed empirically.

strengths: Addresses a genuine limitation in prior articulated-object reconstruction work (restriction to two discrete states and single-joint/known-part-count assumptions) by proposing a latent-conditioned deformation field over a shared canonical Gaussian representation.
Introduces RS-Art, a real-to-sim RGB-D dataset with reverse-engineered part-level 3D models across six object categories, which could be a useful community resource for real-world evaluation.

Extensive experimental coverage: multiple instances per category on an expanded PartNet-Mobility split, objects with 2/3/5 movable parts, robustness to camera pose noise, comparisons against generative articulated-object baselines, and many ablations (refinement stage, number of states, VLM prompting strategy, SAM-based segmentation).
The automatic estimation of part count via VLM prompting removes the need for the manual part-count specification required by several baselines (DTArt, ArtGS).

Consistent quantitative improvements are reported across geometry (Chamfer distance) and kinematic (axis angle/position, part motion) metrics relative to several recent baselines, both on synthetic and real data.
weaknesses: The overall pipeline is a complex, largely non-differentiable, multi-stage combination of existing components (deformable 3DGS, VLM-based counting, K-means trajectory clustering, SAM-based prompting/segmentation, boundary splitting from SAGD) with limited novel methodological insight beyond this engineering integration; the core deformation idea closely resembles existing deformable/dynamic 3DGS work conditioned on a latent code instead of time.

Several key hyperparameters (motion threshold τmot, visibility threshold τvis, minimum cluster size of 2%, number of SAM point prompts) are described as manually tuned on one or two representative instances, raising concerns about generalization, robustness, and reproducibility that are not thoroughly examined via sensitivity analysis.

The evaluation protocol (image budget splitting, per-joint repeated runs for single-joint baselines, provision of ground-truth part counts to multi-part baselines but not to PD2GS) is designed by the authors and could implicitly favor their own method; several baseline failure cases (very large errors, '*' or '–' entries, non-convergence on real data) suggest baselines were not always comparably tuned, inflating the apparent performance gap.

No variance/error bars are reported for PD2GS itself across multiple runs, despite the paper explicitly noting high run-to-run variance in several baselines—this inconsistency limits confidence in the reported numerical margins.

The RS-Art dataset construction relies on substantial manual effort (caliper-based reverse modeling, manual segmentation, manual texture/material authoring in Blender/Isaac Sim) for only 18 objects (3 per category across 6 categories), raising concerns about scalability and diversity for broader future use.

Joint type classification (revolute vs. prismatic) relies on a simple rank-based heuristic with a fixed threshold (r<0.05) and the paper explicitly acknowledges failure to handle screw-type joints, limiting generality of the kinematic modeling.
Comparisons to generative articulated-object priors (NAP, SINGAPO) are dismissed relatively superficially as apples-to-oranges without deeper discussion of complementary strengths/use cases.

The method still assumes accurate known camera poses and cannot handle fully occluded regions, which are significant practical limitations for real-world deployment, and these are only briefly acknowledged rather than addressed.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated formulation: a shared canonical Gaussian field deformed via a latent-conditioned MLP naturally supports arbitrary/continuous interaction states, avoiding the fragmentation and drift of prior two-state/pairwise registration approaches.

The coarse-to-fine part segmentation pipeline (motion-trajectory clustering + VLM-based part-count estimation + visibility-aware SAM prompting + boundary-aware Gaussian splitting) is a clever, fully self-supervised way to obtain sharp, mutually exclusive part boundaries without manual part-count specification, unlike DTArt/ArtGS which require it.

Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple instances per category on an expanded PartNet-Mobility split (addressing a real methodological gap in prior work that often tested one instance/category), plus additional experiments on 3-part and 5-part objects showing robustness to increased kinematic complexity.

Introduction of RS-Art, a real-to-sim RGB-D dataset with reverse-engineered part-level 3D/URDF models, is a valuable and rare resource enabling rigorous real-world evaluation, and results show the method transfers reasonably well to real data despite noise and limited viewpoints.

Extensive ablations and supplementary analyses (refinement stage, number of interaction states K, VLM prompting strategies, SAM segmentation comparisons against SAGD, per-module quantitative breakdown, camera pose noise robustness, comparison with generative articulated baselines NAP/SINGAPO, training/inference timing) substantially strengthen the empirical claims and demonstrate the contribution of individual pipeline components.

Demonstrated qualitative and quantitative advantage over both articulation-specific baselines and general dynamic NeRF/3DGS methods in unseen-state interpolation, showing the framework's utility for digital-twin-style continuous control applications.
Clear, honest discussion of limitations (occlusion, lack of physical properties, screw-joint ambiguity, pose-accuracy dependence) rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Baseline evaluation methodology has some fairness concerns: single-joint baselines are run once per joint and results merged, and the paper reports only the 'first run' for methods with high run-to-run variance rather than averaged/multiple-seed results, which could affect the reliability of the comparison despite the stated justification.

Performance under the strict two-state setting (Table 3) is noticeably worse than with more states, indicating the method's headline advantages partly rely on access to more than two interaction states, which may not always be available in practice.

The pipeline involves many hand-tuned thresholds (τmot, τvis, cluster-size cutoffs, etc.) tuned on one or two representative instances; sensitivity/robustness of the full pipeline to these hyperparameters across diverse objects is not deeply analyzed.
RS-Art, while valuable, is modest in scale (18 objects across 6 categories, 3 instances each), limiting how much can be concluded about broader real-world generalization.
Training time for PD2GS is higher than some baselines (e.g., ArtGS), and while the paper argues inference efficiency is secondary, this trade-off could matter for some downstream applications.
The joint-type classification heuristic (rank-based revolute/prismatic distinction) is acknowledged to struggle with screw-type or more complex joints, limiting generality of the kinematic modeling.
The method still lacks physical properties (mass, friction, compliance) needed for true digital-twin simulation, despite motivating the work partly via digital twin applications.
